primaryText: Dhen vrexi sti Lisavona.
translation: It is not raining in Lisbon.
comment: NEG1 rains at.the Lisbon: the indicative negator as standard negation, (7).

primaryText: Min pas sti Lisavona.
translation: Don't go to Lisbon.
comment: NEG2 you.go at.the Lisbon: negative *min* under the directive operator expresses a preference for worlds where the addressee does not go, (13).

primaryText: Posus anthropus dhen kseyelase sta niata tu!
translation: How many people he cheated in his youth!
comment: how.many men NEG1 cheated in.the youth his; from Espinal (1997). The paper treats negative exclamatives as rhetorical questions uttered with surprise, since they reject the exclamative complementizer *pu*, (23), and receive a quantity rather than a degree reading, (24).

primaryText: Dhen ipie o Yanis kafe?
translation: Didn't Yanis drink coffee?
comment: NEG1 drank the Yanis coffee; from [romero-han-2004]. The paper collapses preposed and non-preposed negation questions, since pro-drop makes them string-identical, (32), the form appears in alternative questions, (33), and *dhen* licenses *akoma* 'yet' and *again*-modification, (34)–(35).

primaryText: Sto kato kato, dhen ine xrisimi ke i vroxi?
translation: After all, isn't rain useful?
comment: at.the down down NEG1 is useful and the rain: under the rhetorical reading the speaker asserts that rain is useful.

primaryText: Q: Pxios dhen efaye to fayito tu? A: Se pxion dhen aresun ta yuvarlakia?
translation: Q: Who didn't eat their food? A: Who doesn't like meatball soup?
context: It is shared knowledge that dad does not like meatball soup.
comment: A rhetorical question in which *dhen* is interpreted canonically: rhetoricity does not always reverse polarity, and positive rhetorical questions reverse it without any negator, (29), so the non-negative reading is an epiphenomenon of rhetoricity, (30).

primaryText: Fovame min efaye ta yuvarlakia o babas.
translation: I fear dad maybe ate the meatball soup.
comment: I.fear NEG2 ate the meatball.soup the dad: expletive *min* is a biased epistemic modal, (43), incompatible with *isos* 'maybe', (42), and merged in the left periphery, since an unmarked subject cannot precede it, (44).

primaryText: Fovame min dhen efaye ta yuvarlakia o babas.
translation: I fear dad maybe didn't eat the meatball soup.
comment: Expletive *min* co-occurs with canonical *dhen*, and the fear is about the negative alternative.

primaryText: Fovame min efaye TIPOTA o babas.
translation: I fear dad maybe ate nothing.
comment: Expletive *min* cannot license the negative concord item *tipota*; adding *dhen* licenses it, (41).

primaryText: Fovame o babas min efaye yuvarlakia.
translation: I fear dad maybe ate meatball soup.
comment: An informationally unmarked subject cannot precede expletive *min*, which is merged outside the TP.

primaryText: Min ksexaso kati, amesos na koroidepsis.
translation: If I forget something, you will immediately mock me.
comment: NEG2 I.forget something immediately SUBJ you.mock: conditional *min* fails to license *tipota*, (46), co-occurs with *dhen*, (47), and is felicitous only for what has happened before, (49), a bias for p-worlds, (50).

primaryText: An akusis kutsobolio, amesos tha erthis.
translation: If you hear about some gossip, you will immediately run.
comment: The *min*-free conditional is unmarked, whereas the variant with *min*, (49a), describes something repetitive, a habit or a norm.

primaryText: Min efaye ta yuvarlakia o babas?
translation: Did dad maybe eat the meatball soup?
comment: Question *min* encodes positive speaker bias, (56), where the *min*-free question, (55b), is attributed to an ignorant speaker; unlike English preposed negation questions, *min*-questions embed, (51b) against (57b).

primaryText: Min dhen efaye ta yuvarlakia o babas?
translation: Did dad maybe not eat the meatball soup?

primaryText: J'ai peur que vous ne vous fassiez piquer par une méduse.
translation: I fear you might get stung by a jellyfish.
comment: From [tahar-2021]: fear-predicate *ne* expresses dispreference, a deontic modal ranking p-worlds, (60).

primaryText: paxadeti še-lo lo yiša'er klum.
translation: I was scared that there would be nothing left.
comment: I.feared that-NEG NEG remain nothing: the expletive marker attaches to the complementizer, above the canonical *lo*. From Francez (to appear: 23, ex. (41)).

primaryText: Mais tul defent ne seit gabeth Quant dit que set e fait que peot.
translation: But you forbid him from being humiliated, he who says what he knows and does what he can.
context: Benedeit, Le voyage de Saint Brendan, 1121.
comment: Under *defent* 'forbid' the subject stops the humiliation: negative predicates share the doxastic component of emotive doxastics, (63). Adapted from Tahar (2022: 45, ex. (34)). The paper prints the title as Le voyage de Saint Bredan.

primaryText: ¿Hay quien dude que no son falsas las tales historias?
translation: Does anybody doubt the falsehood of such stories?
comment: From Espinal (2000): *no* under *dudar* 'doubt' is non-negative; dubitatives involve a doxastic component, (66).

primaryText: apisteis me: ouk episte:me: e:i he: arete:
translation: You doubt that virtue is knowledge.
comment: you.doubt NEG2 NEG1 knowledge is.SUBJ the virtue: expletive *me:*, the ancestor of *min*, above canonical *ou(k)*.

primaryText: Resto qui finché non parli.
translation: I stay here until you talk.
comment: From [tovena-1996]: with the activity *parlare* the negation is visible, my staying ending when your not-speaking ends, while (69b) without *non* means 'while you talk'; with an achievement, (68), the two coincide and *non* looks expletive.

primaryText: Je l'ai fait sans qu'il ne me voie.
translation: I did it without him seeing me.
comment: Proposed to be NEG1 in a negative concord relation with *sans*, (73), since Jamaican *widoutn*, (72), carries no dispreference and *without*-words have no modal component. From Makri (2013: 17, ex. (26)).

primaryText: Me ne andrò a meno che tu non mangi.
translation: I will go away unless you eat.
comment: From Greco (2019: 5, ex. (6)): with *se* 'if' in place of *a meno che*, *non* is standard negation, (76), so the licensor is the negative component of UNLESS, a negative adverbial.

primaryText: Gianni è più alto di quanto non sia Pietro.
translation: Gianni is taller than Peter.
comment: Equivalent to the *non*-free (77′); *non* is the optional spell-out of the negation in the comparative operator, (78), and the epistemic effect comes from the subjunctive.

primaryText: non -ne animadvertis?
translation: Don't you observe?
comment: NEG1 NEG2 you.observe: the interrogative particle *-ne* co-occurs with canonical *non*, like Greek *min dhen*.

primaryText: A: Can I trust you? B: Have I ever hurt your feelings?
comment: A positive rhetorical question conveying the negative assertion: polarity reversal without any negator, so rhetorical questions host NEG1 masked by rhetoricity, (88).

primaryText: Che cosa non ha fatto Gianni!
translation: The things Gianni did!
comment: A quantity reading, as in Greek, (24b), and Hebrew, (89). From Delfitto and Fiorin (2014: 284, ex. (1)).

primaryText: ma še-dani lo katav hitparsem ba-iton.
translation: Whatever Dani wrote was published in the newspaper.
comment: what that-Dani NEG wrote was.published in.the.newspaper: *lo* contributes ignorance or indifference like *-ever*; the alternatives differ in the value of the wh-word and are unranked, so free relatives are not a canonical host. From Eilam (2007: 1, ex. (1)).
